Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe glory of Assyria.1–9Its fall, and the like for Egypt.10–18
Assyria's glory is pictured as a cedar (verses 1–9)

When we see others fall into sin and ruin, we should be warned against pride and false confidence.

The prophet presents an example of a ruler whose greatness resembled that of the king of Egypt.

Assyria is compared with a magnificent cedar tree.

Those who rise above others often become objects of envy.

But the blessings of the heavenly paradise are never spoiled in this way.

The greatest security any created thing can offer is like the shadow of a tree: narrow and fragile protection.

Let us therefore seek our safety with God, where we truly can rest.

We must recognize his hand in the rise of powerful people, rather than envy them.

Though worldly prosperity may appear firmly established, its security is only an appearance.

Assyria's fall warns Egypt (verses 10–18)

The king of Egypt resembled Assyria's king in greatness.

He also resembled him in pride, and would resemble him in ruin.

His own sin caused his downfall.

We lose no earthly comfort that we have not already forfeited many times through sin.

When powerful rulers fall, they often draw many others into destruction with them, just as many powerful rulers have fallen before them.

Their downfall should warn us to remain humble.

Look how low Pharaoh would be brought!

What would remain of his splendor and pride?

It is better to be a lowly tree of righteousness, bearing fruit for God's glory and other people's good.

The wicked may flourish like a tall cedar or a spreading bay tree, but soon they disappear and their place can no longer be found.

Let us observe the upright person: the end of that person is peace.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.31.1-Ezek.31.9]
Chapter 31
The glory of Assyria. ( [Ezek.31.1-Ezek.31.9] Ezek 31:1-9) Its fall, and the like for Egypt. ( [Ezek.31.10-Ezek.31.18] Ezek 31:10-18)
Verses 1-9 The falls of others, both into sin and ruin, warn us not to be secure or high-minded. The prophet is to show an instance of one whom the king of Egypt resembled in greatness, the Assyrian, compared to a stately cedar. Those who excel others, make themselves the objects of envy; but the blessings of the heavenly paradise are not liable to such alloy. The utmost security that any creature can give, is but like the shadow of a tree, a scanty and slender protection. But let us flee to God for protection, there we shall be safe. His hand must be owned in the rising of the great men of the earth, and we must not envy them. Though worldly people may seem to have firm prosperity, yet it only seems so.
[Ezek.31.10-Ezek.31.18]
Verses 10-18 The king of Egypt resembled the king of Assyria in his greatness: here we see he resembles him in his pride. And he shall resemble him in his fall. His own sin brings his ruin. None of our comforts are ever lost, but what have been a thousand times forfeited. When great men fall, many fall with them, as many have fallen before them. The fall of proud men is for warning to others, to keep them humble. See how low Pharaoh lies; and see what all his pomp and pride are come to. It is best to be a lowly tree of righteousness, yielding fruit to the glory of God, and to the good of men. The wicked man is often seen flourishing like the cedar, and spreading like the green bay tree, but he soon passes away, and his place is no more found. Let us then mark the perfect man, and behold the upright, for the end of that man is peace.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe fall of Egypt.1–16It is like that of other nations.17–32
The fall of Egypt is lamented (verses 1–16)

It is fitting for us to weep and tremble on behalf of people who will not weep or tremble for themselves.

In God's judgment, great oppressors are no better than beasts of prey.

People who admire the world's splendor will be astonished when that splendor collapses.

Those who already know how empty earthly things are will be less surprised.

When other people are destroyed by their sins, we too have reason to fear, since we also are guilty.

The instruments of Egypt's destruction were powerful, and the examples of devastation frightening.

Egypt's waters would flow like oil.

Henry understands this as a sign that deep sadness and heaviness would cover the nation.

God can quickly empty people who possess a great abundance of worldly goods.

The more things we depend on for happiness, the more occasions we create for grief when they disappear.

Even the strongest human beings are weak and helpless before God.

The destruction of Egypt pictured the destruction of Christ's enemies.

Egypt joins other nations in the grave (verses 17–32)

Many nations had been devastated and carried down to the grave before Egypt.

In the prophetic picture, they wait to receive Egypt with contempt.

Yet Judah and Jerusalem, although devastated around the same time by the same power, are not included in this list.

The difference lay in God's merciful purpose in correcting his own people and the salvation he had reserved for them.

For Judah, the suffering was not the same final descent into the pit.

Pharaoh would see the other nations and find a kind of consolation.

But the comfort wicked people imagine enjoying after death is only fantasy, not real comfort.

This picture of ruined kingdoms shows how sorrowful the present world is and how strong the rule of death appears in it.

Human beings already die quickly enough, yet they devise ingenious ways to destroy one another.

The passage also makes us look toward the next world.

Although it chiefly concerns the destruction of nations, Henry understands it to contain an unmistakable allusion to the eternal ruin of those who remain unrepentant.

How terribly Satan deceives people!

Why do they commit such evil and shed so much blood in pursuit of wealth, fame, power or pleasure?

Their anxious striving is empty.

The day will come when everyone in the grave hears the voice of Christ and comes out.

Those who have done good will rise to life; those who have done evil will rise to condemnation.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.32.1-Ezek.32.16]
Chapter 32
The fall of Egypt. ( [Ezek.32.1-Ezek.32.16] Ezek 32:1-16) It is like that of other nations. ( [Ezek.32.17-Ezek.32.32] Ezek 32:17-32)
Verses 1-16 It becomes us to weep and tremble for those who will not weep and tremble for themselves. Great oppressors are, in God's account, no better than beasts of prey. Those who admire the pomp of this world, will wonder at the ruin of that pomp; which to those who know the vanity of all things here below, is no surprise. When others are ruined by sin, we have to fear, knowing ourselves guilty. The instruments of the desolation are formidable. And the instances of the desolation are frightful. The waters of Egypt shall run like oil, which signifies there should be universal sadness and heaviness upon the whole nation. God can soon empty those of this world's goods who have the greatest fulness of them. By enlarging the matters of our joy, we increase the occasions of our sorrow. How weak and helpless, as to God, are the most powerful of mankind! The destruction of Egypt was a type of the destruction of the enemies of Christ.
[Ezek.32.17-Ezek.32.32]
Verses 17-32 Divers nations are mentioned as gone down to the grave before Egypt, who are ready to give her a scornful reception; these nations had been lately ruined and wasted. But though Judah and Jerusalem were about this time ruined and laid waste, yet they are not mentioned here. Though they suffered the same affliction, and by the same hand, yet the kind design for which they were afflicted, and the mercy God reserved for them, altered its nature. It was not to them a going down to the pit, as it was to the heathen. Pharaoh shall see, and be comforted; but the comfort wicked ones have after death, is poor comfort, not real, but only in fancy. The view this prophecy gives of ruined states shows something of this present world, and the empire of death in it. Come and see the calamitous state of human life. As if men did not die fast enough, they are ingenious at finding out ways to destroy one another. Also of the other world; though the destruction of nations as such, seems chiefly intended, here is plain allusion to the everlasting ruin of impenitent sinners. How are men deceived by Satan! What are the objects they pursue through scenes of bloodshed, and their many sins? Surely man disquiets himself in vain, whether he pursues wealth, fame, power, or pleasure. The hour cometh, when all that are in their graves shall hear the voice of Christ, and shall come forth; those that have done good to the resurrection of life, and those that have done evil to the resurrection of damnation.

Ezekiel must warn people in danger (verses 1–9)

The prophet is a watchman for the house of Israel.

His work is to warn sinners about their misery and danger and call them to abandon wickedness and live.

If people perish because he neglects that duty, he brings guilt upon himself.

Consider the responsibility borne by those who excuse sin, flatter sinners and encourage them to suppose they will enjoy peace while persisting in evil.

Human beings often show far greater wisdom about temporary dangers than about spiritual dangers.

They appoint guards for houses and sentries to warn of approaching enemies.

Yet when their everlasting happiness or misery is at stake, they resent ministers who faithfully obey the Master's command to warn them.

They would rather perish while listening to pleasant assurances.

God offers mercy to those who repent (verses 10–20)

God answered those who despaired of receiving mercy with a solemn declaration of his readiness to forgive.

The destruction of Jerusalem and its government had been determined.

But that did not determine the eternal destiny of every individual.

God promises life to the righteous.

Yet people who have made an outward profession of faith may ruin themselves through proud confidence in their own righteousness.

Depending on themselves, they fall into sin.

By contrast, people who have lived wicked lives may repent, abandon their evil conduct and be saved.

God's grace has brought about many astonishing and blessed changes like this.

When a person makes a settled break with sin, the separation between that person and God also ends.

Judah fails to learn from its ruin (verses 21–29)

People are deeply resistant to instruction when they do not recognize their dependence upon God even after every created comfort has failed them.

Many claim the special promises given to true believers while their conduct proves them to be God's enemies.

They call their unfounded expectation strong faith.

But God's own testimony declares that they have earned the warnings of judgment rather than the promised blessings.

Hearers do not necessarily obey God's word (verses 30–33)

People often come to faithful preaching for unworthy or selfish reasons.

Some attend merely to find something to criticize.

Far more come because of curiosity or habit.

Nevertheless, God can change their hearts.

Whether people listen or refuse, the outcome will eventually show that God's servant was among them.

Those who fail to appreciate God's mercies by making good use of them may justly discover their value only when those mercies are taken away.
classic_reading:

Ezekiel's duty as a watchman. ( [Ezek.33.1-Ezek.33.9] Ezek 33:1-9) He is to vindicate the Divine government. ( [Ezek.33.10-Ezek.33.20] Ezek 33:10-20) The desolation of Judea. ( [Ezek.33.21-Ezek.33.29] Ezek 33:21-29) Judgments on the mockers of the prophets. ( [Ezek.33.30-Ezek.33.33] Ezek 33:30-33)

Verses 21-29 Those are unteachable indeed, who do not learn their dependence upon God, when all creature-comforts fail. Many claim an interest in the peculiar blessings to true believers, while their conduct proves them enemies of God. They call this groundless presumption strong faith, when God's testimony declares them entitled to his threatenings, and nothing else.
[Ezek.33.30-Ezek.33.33]
Verses 30-33 Unworthy and corrupt motives often lead men to the places where the word of God is faithfully preached. Many come to find somewhat to oppose: far more come of curiosity or mere habit. Men may have their hearts changed. But whether men hear or forbear, they will know by the event that a servant of God has been among them. All who will not know the worth of mercies by the improvement of them, will justly be made to know their worth by the want of them.

Israel's shepherds neglect the flock (verses 1–6)

The people became like sheep without a shepherd.

Their enemies preyed upon them, and their land was left desolate.

No official position or high social rank places anyone beyond the correction of God's word.

Those who neglect the duties of their office and misuse the trust others have placed in them deserve rebuke.

The Lord gathers and cares for his flock (verses 7–16)

God announced that he intended mercy toward his scattered sheep.

The promise first concerned the restoration of the Jews to their own land.

It also pictured the Good Shepherd's tender care for his people's souls.

He finds them in the darkness of ignorance and leads them into his fold.

He comes to their aid in persecution and temptation.

He guides them along righteous paths and gives them rest in his love and faithfulness.

Proud, self-sufficient people oppose the true gospel and those who trust it; we must guard against their influence.

The Shepherd provides rest for troubled believers but terror for presumptuous sinners.

Christ's kingdom brings pasture and blessing (verses 17–31)

The whole nation appeared to be the Lord's flock.

But the people differed greatly in their character, and he knew how to distinguish them.

Good pasture and deep water picture the pure word of God and the practice of justice.

Henry understands verses 23–31 as a prophecy of Christ and of the most glorious periods of his church on earth.

Under Christ, the Good Shepherd, the church becomes a blessing to those around it.

Though Christ was excellent in himself, he appeared like a tender plant growing from dry ground.

As the Tree of Life, bearing every fruit of salvation, he gives spiritual nourishment to his people.

We should constantly pray for showers of blessing wherever Christ's truth is preached and for everyone who professes the gospel to be filled with the fruits of righteousness.

The rulers reproved. ( [Ezek.34.1-Ezek.34.6] Ezek 34:1-6) The people are to be restored to their own land. ( [Ezek.34.7-Ezek.34.16] Ezek 34:7-16) The kingdom of Christ. ( [Ezek.34.17-Ezek.34.31] Ezek 34:17-31)
Verses 1-6 The people became as sheep without a shepherd, were given up as a prey to their enemies, and the land was utterly desolated. No rank or office can exempt from the reproofs of God's word, men who neglect their duty, and abuse the trust reposed in them.
[Ezek.34.7-Ezek.34.16]
Verses 7-16 The Lord declared that he intended mercy towards the scattered flock. Doubtless this, in the first place, had reference to the restoration of the Jews. It also represented the good Shepherd's tender care of the souls of his people. He finds them in their days of darkness and ignorance, and brings them to his fold. He comes to their relief in times of persecution and temptation. He leads them in the ways of righteousness, and causes them to rest on his love and faithfulness. The proud and self-sufficient, are enemies of the true gospel and of believers; against such we must guard. He has rest for disquieted saints, and terror for presumptuous sinners.
[Ezek.34.17-Ezek.34.31]
Verses 17-31 The whole nation seemed to be the Lord's flock, yet they were very different characters; but he knew how to distinguish between them. By good pastures and deep waters, are meant the pure word of God and the dispensing of justice. The latter verses, 23-31, prophesy of Christ, and of the most glorious times of his church on earth. Under Him, as the good Shepherd, the church would be a blessing to all around. Christ, though excellent in himself, was as a tender plant out of a dry ground. Our constant desire and prayer should be, that there may be showers of blessings in every place where the truth of Christ is preached; and that all who profess the gospel may be filled with fruits of righteousness.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A prophecy against Edom.

Edom's hatred will bring desolation (verses 1–9)

Anyone who has God against them also has God's word against them.

Those who cultivate unrelenting hatred toward God and his people display the attitude of the sinful human mind.

If they continue in it, they can expect only lasting desolation.

Edom's boastful words are known to God (verses 10–15)

When we see the vanity of this world revealed through other people's disappointments, losses and hardships, we should become less attached to possessions, not more eager to seize them.

God knows every word we speak, even the most idle.

The boldest and most defiant expression is not beyond his rebuke.

Through the defeat of his church's enemies, the Lord intends his own glory.

We may be certain that he will accomplish his purpose.

Henry looks forward to the fullness of Jews and Gentiles entering Christ's church, when opposition characterized by anti-Christian hostility will finally be removed.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.35.1-Ezek.35.9]
Chapter 35
A prophecy against Edom.
Verses 1-9 All who have God against them, have the word of God against them. Those that have a constant hatred to God and his people, as the carnal mind has, can only expect to be made desolate for ever.
[Ezek.35.10-Ezek.35.15]
Verses 10-15 When we see the vanity of the world in the disappointments, losses, and crosses, which others meet with, instead of showing ourselves greedy of worldly things, we should sit more loose to them. In the multitude of words, not one is unknown to God; not the most idle word; and the most daring is not above his rebuke. In the destruction of the enemies of the church, God designs his own glory; and we may be sure that he will not come short of his design. And when the fulness of the Jews and Gentiles shall come into the church, all antichristian opposers shall be destroyed.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe land shall be delivered from heathen oppressors.1–15The people are reminded of former sins, and promised deliverance.16–24Also holiness, and gospel blessings.25–38
The land will be delivered from its oppressors (verses 1–15)

Those who treat God's people with contempt and reproach will find that the same disgrace returns upon themselves.

God promises to show favor to his Israel. We need not complain if, as human beings grow more unkind, God shows us still greater kindness.

His people will return to their own borders.

This return was also a picture of the heavenly Canaan, which belongs to all God's children and into which they will be gathered together.

When God graciously returns to a people and they return to him in obedience, their grievances will be put right.

Henry expects the complete fulfillment of this prophecy in a future event.

Former sins and promised deliverance (verses 16–24)

The restoration of Israel pictures our redemption through Christ. It shows that the ultimate purpose of salvation is God's glory.

A people's sin defiles their land. It makes the land offensive to God and unpleasant for those who live there.

God's holy name is his great name. His holiness is his greatness; nothing else makes a human being truly great.

A clean heart and the blessings of the gospel (verses 25–38)

Water pictures the cleansing of souls polluted by sin. Yet water itself can remove only outward bodily uncleanness.

Henry understands water generally as the sacramental sign of the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work. That work is always connected with the atoning blood of Christ.

When Christ's blood is applied by faith to the conscience, cleansing it from evil works, the Holy Spirit also works in the powers of the soul to remove sin's pollution.

Everyone who belongs to the new covenant receives a new heart and a new spirit and is enabled to walk in newness of life.

God promises to give a heart of flesh: a gentle, tender heart responsive to his holy will.

Renewing grace changes a soul as profoundly as if a lifeless stone became living flesh.

God places his Spirit within his people as their Teacher, Guide and Sanctifier.

His promise to give the grace we need for obedience should encourage us to keep seeking and practicing our duty.

These promises may be pleaded in prayer by all true believers in every age, and God will fulfill them.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.36.1-Ezek.36.15]
Chapter 36
The land shall be delivered from heathen oppressors. ( [Ezek.36.1-Ezek.36.15] Ezek 36:1-15) The people are reminded of former sins, and promised deliverance. ( [Ezek.36.16-Ezek.36.24] Ezek 36:16-24) Also holiness, and gospel blessings. ( [Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.38] Ezek 36:25-38)
Verses 1-15 Those who put contempt and reproach on God's people, will have them turned on themselves. God promises favour to his Israel. We have no reason to complain, if the more unkind men are, the more kind God is. They shall come again to their own border. It was a type of the heavenly Canaan, of which all God's children are heirs, and into which they all shall be brought together. And when God returns in mercy to a people who return to him in duty, all their grievances will be set right. The full completion of this prophecy must be in some future event.
[Ezek.36.16-Ezek.36.24]
Verses 16-24 The restoration of that people, being typical of our redemption by Christ, shows that the end aimed at in our salvation is the glory of God. The sin of a people defiles their land; renders it abominable to God, and uncomfortable to themselves. God's holy name is his great name; his holiness is his greatness, nor does any thing else make a man truly great.
[Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.38]
Verses 25-38 Water is an emblem of the cleansing our polluted souls from sin. But no water can do more than take away the filth of the flesh. Water seems in general the sacramental sign of the sanctifying influences of the Holy Ghost; yet this is always connected with the atoning blood of Christ. When the latter is applied by faith to the conscience, to cleanse it from evil works, the former is always applied to the powers of the soul, to purify it from the pollution of sin. All that have an interest in the new covenant, have a new heart and a new spirit, in order to their walking in newness of life. God would give a heart of flesh, a soft and tender heart, complying with his holy will. Renewing grace works as great a change in the soul, as the turning a dead stone into living flesh. God will put his Spirit within, as a Teacher, Guide, and Sanctifier. The promise of God's grace to fit us for our duty, should quicken our constant care and endeavour to do our duty. These are promises to be pleaded by, and will be fulfilled to, all true believers in every age.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod restores dried bones to life.1–14The whole house of Israel is represented as enjoying the blessings of Christ's kingdom.15–28
God raises dry bones to life (verses 1–14)

No created power can restore dead human bones to life. God alone can make them live.

In the vision, skin and flesh covered the bones. Then the wind was commanded to blow upon the bodies, and they came to life.

The wind pictured God's Spirit and his power to give life.

This vision encouraged the discouraged Jews. It foretold both their restoration after the captivity and their recovery from the long dispersion that continued in Henry's day.

It also clearly pointed toward the resurrection of the dead.

The same vision represents God's powerful grace in converting even the most hopeless sinners.

Let us turn to the Lord who will one day open our graves and bring us out to judgment. May he deliver us from sin now, place his Spirit within us and keep us through faith by his power until salvation.

Judah and Israel united under Christ (verses 15–28)

The symbolic action showed that the Lord would unite Judah and Israel.

Christ is the true David, the King of Israel.

Those whom Christ makes willing through his power he also leads to obey his judgments and keep his commandments.

Henry says future events will explain this prophecy further.

Few things have hindered the spread of the gospel more than divisions among believers.

Let us therefore maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Let us seek divine grace to avoid detestable things.

And let us pray that all nations become obedient and happy subjects of the Son of David, so that the Lord will be our God and we will be his people forever.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.14]
Chapter 37
God restores dried bones to life. ( [Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.14] Ezek 37:1-14) The whole house of Israel is represented as enjoying the blessings of Christ's kingdom. ( [Ezek.37.15-Ezek.37.28] Ezek 37:15-28)
Verses 1-14 No created power could restore human bones to life. God alone could cause them to live. Skin and flesh covered them, and the wind was then told to blow upon these bodies; and they were restored to life. The wind was an emblem of the Spirit of God, and represented his quickening powers. The vision was to encourage the desponding Jews; to predict both their restoration after the captivity, and also their recovery from their present and long-continued dispersion. It was also a clear intimation of the resurrection of the dead; and it represents the power and grace of God, in the conversion of the most hopeless sinners to himself. Let us look to Him who will at last open our graves, and bring us forth to judgment, that He may now deliver us from sin, and put his Spirit within us, and keep us by his power, through faith, unto salvation.
[Ezek.37.15-Ezek.37.28]
Verses 15-28 This emblem was to show the people, that the Lord would unite Judah and Israel. Christ is the true David, Israel's King of old; and those whom he makes willing in the day of his power, he makes to walk in his judgments, and to keep his statutes. Events yet to come will further explain this prophecy. Nothing has more hindered the success of the gospel than divisions. Let us study to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; let us seek for Divine grace to keep us from detestable things; and let us pray that all nations may be obedient and happy subjects of the Son of David, that the Lord may be our God, and we may be his people for evermore.

Gog and the hostile army (verses 1–13)

These events belong to the latter days.

Henry says it is supposed that these enemies will unite to invade Judea and that God will defeat them.

God not only knows who is presently hostile to his church; he also knows who will become its enemies.

Through his word, he warns them that he is against them.

Even if the wicked join together, they will not escape his judgment.

God's judgment and protection (verses 14–23)

The enemy would launch a formidable attack upon Israel.

When Israel dwells safely under God's protection, the attackers will discover how useless their attempts to destroy it are.

God's word contains promises of security that his people may treasure in advance of dangers and troubles facing the church in the latter days.

In judging sinners, God makes his greatness and holiness known.

We should therefore pray daily:

Father, glorify your own name.
classic_reading:

Verses 1-13 These events will be in the latter days. It is supposed these enemies will come together to invade the land of Judea, and God will defeat them. God not only sees who are now the enemies of his church, but he foresees who will be so, and lets them know by his word that he is against them; though they join together, the wicked shall not be unpunished.

In the destruction of sinners, God makes it appear that he is a great and holy God. We should desire and pray daily. Father, glorify thine own name.

Gog's army is destroyed (verses 1–10)

The Lord will make even the most careless and hardened sinners acknowledge his holy name, either through his righteous judgment or through the abundance of his mercy and grace.

Weapons formed against Zion will not succeed.

Henry regards this prophecy as certain, although its fulfillment belongs to the latter days.

From its language, he concludes that Gog's army appears to be destroyed by a miracle.

The scale of the destruction and the work of cleansing (verses 11–22)

God will destroy a vast number of enemies to defend his people Israel.

Times of extraordinary deliverance should also be times of reform.

Everyone should do everything possible to remove what disgraces the land.

Sin is an enemy against which every person should struggle.

Those entrusted with public work, especially the work of cleansing and reforming a country, should be persistent and finish what they begin.

Whenever good work is needed, everyone should help it forward.

Receiving extraordinary favor from God should move us to cleanse ourselves from all evil.

This requires determined effort, including a careful search into the hidden corners of sin.

God's judgments against sin and sinners are a sacrifice to his justice and a feast to the faith and hope of his people.

Sin's consequences can pursue people even after their death.

After all the wealth and honor ambitious, greedy people pursue, a burial place may be all that remains to them on earth, while those who die guilty face misery in the world to come.

Israel receives God's favor again (verses 23–29)

Henry looks forward to God's showing mercy to the whole house of Israel through their conversion to Christianity.

After Israel bears the shame of having been rejected because of sin, the nations will learn to know, worship and serve the Lord.

Israel too will know him as revealed in and through Christ.

Henry expressly says past events do not fully answer this prediction.

The outpouring of God's Spirit is a pledge that his favor will continue.

He will no longer hide his face from those upon whom he pours out his Spirit.

When we pray that God never cast us from his presence, let us pray just as earnestly that he never take his Holy Spirit from us.

Every one should help the utmost he can, toward cleansing the land from reproach. Sin is an enemy every man should strive against. Those engaged in public work, especially of cleansing and reforming a land, ought to be men who will go through with what they undertake, who will be always employed. When good work is to be done, every one should further it. Having received special favours from God, let us cleanse ourselves from all evil. It is a work which will require persevering diligence, that search may be made into the secret recesses of sin. The judgments of the Lord, brought upon sin and sinners, are a sacrifice to the justice of God, and a feast to the faith and hope of God's people. See how evil pursues sinners, even after death. modern_osis:
Original heading

The Vision of the Temple.

The temple vision and its meaning

This chapter begins a vision that continues through Ezekiel 48, at the end of the book.

Henry rightly regards it as one of the most difficult passages in Scripture.

When we cannot resolve a difficult passage, we should thank God that our salvation does not depend upon understanding every detail of it.

Everything necessary for salvation has been made sufficiently clear.

We should patiently wait for God to reveal what we cannot yet understand.

This chapter describes the two outer courts of the temple.

Henry says it is unclear whether the figure Ezekiel sees is the Son of God or a created angel.

What is certain is that Christ is both our Altar and our Sacrifice.

We should look to him in faith whenever we approach God.

Christ is salvation in the midst of the earth (Psalm 74:12), and people may look to him from every direction.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.40.1]
Chapter 40
The Vision of the Temple.
Here is a vision, beginning at Ezek 40, and continued to the end of the book, Ezek 48, which is justly looked upon to be one of the most difficult portions in all the book of God. When we despair to be satisfied as to any difficulty we meet with, let us bless God that our salvation does not depend upon it, but that things necessary are plain enough; and let us wait till God shall reveal even this unto us. This chapter describes two outward courts of the temple. Whether the personage here mentioned was the Son of God, or a created angel, is not clear. But Christ is both our Altar and our Sacrifice, to whom we must look with faith in all approaches to God; and he is Salvation in the midst of the earth, Ps. 74:12, to be looked unto from all quarters.
